title: Air India Fully Refunded His Non-Refundable Tickets After a Family Medical Emergency
excerpt: Hardik Rajgor expected nothing when he asked for an exception. Air India asked for documents, refunded the tickets in full, and its executives called to wish the patient a speedy recovery.
body:
• Traveller Hardik Rajgor cancelled a trip days before travel after a serious family medical emergency required tests and immediate surgery — on tickets that were explicitly non-refundable.
  • He asked Air India for an exception anyway; the airline requested documents to verify the case, then offered a full refund.
  • Two Air India executives also called him personally to wish the patient a speedy recovery. No route or refund amount was disclosed.
  • The outcome matches policy: medical emergencies with documentation are a recognised exception to non-refundable fares, and India's DGCA norms entitle passengers to a refund or credit shell in such cases.

The fare rules said no. When Hardik Rajgor had to cancel a trip a few days before travel because a serious medical situation arose in his family — tests to be run, then a surgery to be scheduled immediately — his Air India tickets were non-refundable, and he knew it. He contacted the airline anyway, explained the circumstances and asked whether an exception could be made.

"Wasn't expecting much," he wrote in a post on X on October 20 that News18 reported. What happened next is why the post travelled. Air India asked him for a few documents to assess that the case was genuine, then offered a full refund. A couple of the airline's executives also called him personally to wish the patient a speedy recovery.

"I really appreciate it. They didn't have to, but they made that extra effort."

— Hardik Rajgor, traveller, on X

Rajgor credited the "soft human touch," saying it separates Indian brands from many others in the world. Air India replied publicly, thanking him for his words, saying it was glad it could assist during a difficult time, wishing the patient good health and saying it looked forward to serving him again. News18 noted the account is based on Rajgor's own post and has not been independently verified by the outlet; the article discloses no route, dates or refund amount.

Why this was not pure generosity

It was discretionary in manner but not in principle. Medical emergencies are the standing exception in airline refund practice: as SkyRefund's Air India policy guide summarises, a passenger who cannot fly because of an urgent health condition can generally cancel without fee and receive a full refund on providing valid medical documentation, with similar treatment for the death of a passenger or immediate family member. India's aviation regulator goes further on paper: under the DGCA's revised refund norms, a ticket cancelled because the passenger or a co-traveller on the same booking had a medical emergency and was hospitalised during the travel period qualifies for a refund or a credit shell, and the norms also give every passenger a 48-hour look-in window to cancel or change without extra charges on bookings made well ahead of departure.

The lesson for travellers

Most travellers in Rajgor's position never ask — "non-refundable" reads as final. The working sequence from this case: contact the airline before departure, state the emergency plainly, attach documentation before being asked twice, and keep the request in writing. Airlines assess genuineness, not worthiness; a documented emergency, raised early, is exactly the case the exception exists for. Whether the refund lands as cash to the original payment method or a credit shell can vary — Rajgor's was a full refund — but the first step is always the ask.

steps.detail: Explain the emergency and ask for an exception while the booking is still active — no-shows are far harder to refund.
Airlines assess genuineness: expect to provide medical documents showing the emergency, as Air India requested in this case.
A written request through the airline's official channels creates a record; keep the PNR and all replies.
Under India's revised DGCA norms, cancellation for your own or a co-traveller's medical emergency makes you eligible for a refund or credit shell — cite it if the first answer is no.
